To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the red edge optical indices R/sub 750/R/sub 710/ and R/sub 750/ (1-R/sub 750/), used in the merit function of the numerical inversion, perform better than all the spectral bands from hyper-spectral CASI data for chlorophyl content estimation in closed canopies, and that the effect of shadows, and LAI variation is minimized by using these indices.
the use of the red-edge optical indices in the inversion of the SAILH model for chlorophyll estimation in sugar maples was successful.
the red edge optical indices are the best parameters for chlorophyll estimation in dense forest canopies with narrowband optical sensors.
In summary, our research is concerned with

the development of new methodologies and models to link leaf to hyper-spectral canopy reflectance data through scaling-up approaches, and the use of numerical inversion of the radiative transfer models to estimate chlorophyll content.

the following objectives: (1) to develop an inversion method for canopy reflectance model parameters, including chlorophyll content, using a hyper-spectral data set, (2) to evaluate the performance of the model inversion method, (3) to develop a scaling-up approach for chlorophyll estimation, (4) to evaluate the effect of the canopy model on the accuracy of the scaling-up approach, (5) to develop a new approach for the estimation of chlorophyll content in a forest

the following objectives: to study the scaling-up and numerical inversion methodologies for chlorophyll estimation in closed and dense canopies of Acer Saccharum M., and to evaluate the performance of the different methodologies for chlorophyl1 content estimation in closed and densely forested stands of Acer saccharin M. in the Algoma region.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the use of red-edge optical indices for chlorphyll content estimation in dense forest canopies with hyper-spectral data is more robust and accurate than the use of single spectral reflectance bands.

the best results for chlorophyll estimation were achieved when the red edge optical index R/sub 750//-R/sub 710/, the PROSPECT model, and the canopy radiative transfer models SAILH and/or MCRM were used.

the scaling-up approach with the SAILH model and the model inversion approach with MCRM model were the best approaches to retrieve chlorophyll content in Acer saccharum forest canopies from hyper-spectral CASI data.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the scaling-up and model inversion approaches are promising for estimating chlorophyll content at the canopy scale, and that the use of narrowband red edge optical indices in the numerical inversion approach is the best option to estimate chlorophyll content in closed canopies.

the scaling-up method using the infinite reflectance formulae and the SAILH model is a simple approach that provides a good estimate of the canopy chlorophyll content with an RMSE=0.3 and R/sub 750//-R/sub 710// chlorophyll index, and the numerical inversion method using the PROSPECT model provides a better estimate of the canopy content with an RMSEE=0.15 and a R/sub 750/-R/sub 710//-chlorophyll index

the scaling-up method is the most appropriate for chlorophyll estimation at canopy level with hyper-spectral airborne data, and that the model inversion method is the most accurate for chlorophyll estimations at leaf level with hyper-spectra of the same species.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the red edge optical index R/sub 750/ / R/sub 710/, which has been widely used in the past, can be applied in the context of the canopy radiative transfer modeling for chlorophyll estimation.

the scaling-up approach is more efficient and reliable than the numerical model inversion approach, especially when the canopy is optically thick and when the canopy is not fully closed and shadows are present, which is the case for many forests in Canada.
the red edge optical indices can be used to estimate leaf chlorophyll content at the canopy level with hyper-spectral data and radiative transfer theory.
